photovoltaics-001.question: When light falls on a pn-junction solar cell, which correctly describes how electrical power can be delivered to an external circuit?
choices: Light heats the junction, and the thermoelectric voltage (Seebeck effect) created by the temperature difference between the p and n sides drives a current proportional to that difference through the external load
A forward voltage is applied with an external supply, and the forward current increased by light is delivered to the load, so without a supply no power can be obtained at all
Electron-hole pairs created by light are separated toward the n and p sides by the built-in field, and under a forward voltage a current opposite to the diode's forward current flows through the load
photovoltaics-001.explanation: When minority carriers generated by light diffuse to the junction, the built-in field of the depletion region sends electrons to the n side and holes to the p side. This is the photocurrent, and with the terminals open, electrons collect on the n side and holes on the p side, producing a forward voltage. With a load connected, the voltage stays in the forward direction while the current flows opposite to the diode's forward current, so the cell operates in the quadrant where the product of current and voltage is negative (power is delivered). No external supply is needed, and the effect is distinct from the thermoelectric effect of a temperature difference. Photodiodes at zero bias use the same photovoltaic effect, but solar cells are designed to deliver power over a large area.

photovoltaics-002.question: Which correctly describes the standard test conditions (STC) used to compare solar-cell performance?
choices: An irradiance of 1000 W/m² with the air mass 1.5 spectrum (about 1.5 times the vertical path through the atmosphere) and a cell temperature of 25 °C
The extraterrestrial spectrum (air mass 0) at the solar constant of about 1360 W/m² and a cell temperature of 0 °C
The air mass 1.5 spectrum at an irradiance of 100 W/m² and an ambient temperature of 25 °C, with the cell temperature left to rise under the sunlight
photovoltaics-002.explanation: Air mass (AM) expresses the path of sunlight through the atmosphere relative to 1 for overhead sun, and is roughly 1/cos θ at a zenith angle θ. AM1.5 corresponds to a zenith angle of about 48°, and as a representative terrestrial condition, the AM1.5G spectrum, which includes scattered light, is set to 1000 W/m² (= 100 mW/cm²) and the cell temperature to 25 °C. The extraterrestrial AM0 spectrum (about 1360 W/m²) is used to evaluate solar cells for satellites. Outdoors the cell temperature rises and efficiency falls, so the temperature is specified for the cell itself rather than the ambient air. 100 W/m² is an order-of-magnitude error.

photovoltaics-003.question: Which correctly describes the quantities used with the current-voltage (I-V) characteristic of a solar cell?
choices: The maximum power is the product of the open-circuit voltage V_oc and the short-circuit current I_sc, and the load resistance is chosen as V_oc/I_sc to obtain this power
The fill factor FF is the maximum power P_max divided by the product of V_oc and I_sc; it expresses how square the I-V curve is and is less than 1
The open-circuit voltage is the voltage at the point of maximum current, and the short-circuit current is the current at the point of maximum voltage; the power is maximum at both points
photovoltaics-003.explanation: Shorting the terminals gives the short-circuit current I_sc at zero voltage, and opening them gives the open-circuit voltage V_oc at zero current. At both points either voltage or current is 0, so the power is 0, and between them lies the maximum power point (V_mp, I_mp) where the product of current and voltage is largest. The fill factor is FF = V_mpI_mp/(V_ocI_sc), the ratio of the area of the maximum-power rectangle drawn inside the I-V curve to that of the rectangle formed by V_oc and I_sc. Because of the exponential diode characteristic it never reaches 1, and good crystalline silicon cells have values around 0.8. V_oc × I_sc cannot actually be extracted, and the conversion efficiency is η = V_ocI_scFF/P_in.

photovoltaics-004.question: For a solar cell that follows the ideal diode equation J = J_sc − J₀[exp(qV/kT) − 1] with a short-circuit current density J_sc = 40 mA/cm² and a saturation current density J₀ = 1.0×10⁻¹² A/cm², which is closest to the open-circuit voltage? (Temperature 300 K, kT/q = 0.0259 V.)
choices: About 0.27 V
About 0.63 V
About 1.1 V
photovoltaics-004.explanation: Setting J = 0 gives V_oc = (kT/q) ln(J_sc/J₀ + 1). J_sc/J₀ = 0.040/1.0×10⁻¹² = 4.0×10¹⁰, whose natural logarithm is about 24.4, so V_oc ≈ 0.0259 × 24.4 ≈ 0.63 V. About 0.27 V wrongly uses the common logarithm (about 10.6), and about 1.1 V corresponds to the bandgap of silicon; the open-circuit voltage is always smaller than the bandgap divided by q. Because V_oc is set by the logarithm of J₀, every tenfold reduction in J₀ through lower recombination raises it by about 60 mV (= 0.0259 × ln10). Keeping J₀ low with surface passivation and high-quality crystals is the key to a high V_oc.

photovoltaics-005.question: A solar cell with an open-circuit voltage of 0.70 V, a short-circuit current density of 40 mA/cm² and a fill factor of 0.80 is measured under standard test conditions (irradiance 100 mW/cm²). Which is closest to the conversion efficiency?
choices: About 28%
About 18%
About 22%
photovoltaics-005.explanation: The maximum power density is V_oc × J_sc × FF = 0.70 V × 40 mA/cm² × 0.80 = 22.4 mW/cm². Dividing by the incident 100 mW/cm² gives a conversion efficiency of 22.4%, about 22%. About 28% forgets the fill factor and treats the product of V_oc and J_sc as extractable power; in reality the power is 0 at the open-circuit and short-circuit points. About 18% applies the fill factor twice. Because efficiency is the product of 3 quantities, raising V_oc (reducing recombination), raising J_sc (reducing reflection and incomplete absorption) and raising FF (reducing series resistance and leakage) are all ways to raise it.

photovoltaics-006.question: Which correctly describes the effects of a solar cell's series resistance R_s and parallel (shunt) resistance R_sh on its I-V characteristic?
choices: A large R_s flattens the curve on the open-circuit-voltage side and a small R_sh makes the current fall with voltage on the short-circuit side; both lower the fill factor
A larger R_s lowers the open-circuit voltage and a larger R_sh lowers the short-circuit current, so both series and parallel resistance should be as small as possible
Neither R_s nor R_sh has any effect in the open-circuit state because no current flows, so they do not affect the open-circuit voltage or fill factor and lower only the short-circuit current
photovoltaics-006.explanation: Series resistance is the resistance met by current flowing through the electrodes and semiconductor; the larger the current, the more voltage IR_s it consumes, so the curve flattens from the maximum power point toward the open-circuit side and the fill factor falls. In the open-circuit state the current is 0, so R_s does not affect the open-circuit voltage. Parallel resistance is a leakage path that bypasses the junction; if it is small, a leakage current V/R_sh proportional to voltage flows and the curve tilts on the short-circuit side. Leakage steals generated current, so under weak light with a small photocurrent the open-circuit voltage also drops greatly. A good solar cell has small R_s and large R_sh; saying that smaller R_sh is better is backwards. Leakage current flows through R_sh even in the open-circuit state, so saying that neither affects the open-circuit voltage and fill factor is also wrong.

photovoltaics-007.question: Which is the general change when the temperature of a crystalline silicon solar cell rises? (Illumination conditions are unchanged.)
choices: The thermal energy kT of the carriers increases, so the open-circuit voltage rises, and the short-circuit current also increases, so the efficiency rises with temperature
Only the short-circuit current changes with temperature; the open-circuit voltage and fill factor are set by the bandgap and do not depend on it, so efficiency stays nearly constant
The saturation current J₀ rises steeply, so the open-circuit voltage falls (about 2 mV per K); the short-circuit current rises slightly, but overall efficiency falls
photovoltaics-007.explanation: The saturation current rises steeply with temperature, as J₀ ∝ nᵢ² ∝ T³exp(−Eg/kT), and in V_oc ≈ (kT/q) ln(J_sc/J₀) the decrease inside the logarithm outweighs the increase in kT/q, so the open-circuit voltage falls. For crystalline silicon this is about −2 mV per K, and the temperature coefficient of efficiency, in relative terms, is said to be roughly −0.3 to −0.5 %/K (depending on the cell structure). As temperature rises the bandgap narrows slightly and absorption at long wavelengths increases, so the short-circuit current rises a little, but the voltage drop has a much larger effect. The fill factor also falls with temperature. Outdoors the cell runs considerably hotter than the ambient air, so module heat dissipation affects energy yield.

photovoltaics-008.question: Which correctly describes the idea behind the theoretical upper limit on the conversion efficiency of a single-junction solar cell (the Shockley–Queisser limit)?
choices: It assumes that all photons with energy above the bandgap are absorbed and all of their energy is converted to electricity, so the limit approaches 100% as the bandgap is made smaller and more light is absorbed
It assumes 1 electron-hole pair per photon, excess energy lost as heat and only radiative recombination, derived from detailed balance; for AM1.5G it is about 33% near 1.3 eV
The limit is simply the Carnot efficiency of about 95% set by the sun's surface temperature of about 5800 K and the cell temperature of 300 K, independent of bandgap
photovoltaics-008.explanation: Shockley and Queisser derived the single-junction efficiency limit from the detailed balance of light absorption and emission between the solar cell and the sun. The major losses are the transmission of light with energy below the bandgap Eg and the conversion of the excess energy of photons above Eg into heat by carrier thermalization. A smaller Eg absorbs more light but lowers the voltage, while a larger Eg raises the voltage but absorbs less light, so for AM1.5G the maximum of about 33% occurs near 1.3–1.4 eV. Radiative recombination, by which the cell itself emits light, cannot be avoided, so the open-circuit voltage is also smaller than Eg/q. The Carnot efficiency of about 95% is the limit for heat engines, not for single-junction solar cells.

photovoltaics-009.question: A silicon solar cell with a bandgap of 1.12 eV absorbs a photon with a wavelength of 500 nm. Roughly what percentage of the photon energy is lost as heat when the resulting electron and hole relax (thermalize) to the band edges? (E[eV] ≈ 1240/λ[nm].)
choices: About 55%
About 45%
Almost 0% (the excess energy creates a 2nd electron-hole pair)
photovoltaics-009.explanation: The photon energy is 1240/500 ≈ 2.48 eV. Electrons and holes relax to the band edges within a short time of a ps or less by emitting phonons, so the 2.48 − 1.12 = 1.36 eV above Eg becomes heat, a fraction of 1.36/2.48 ≈ 0.55, about 55%. About 45% is the fraction 1.12/2.48 that remains at the band edges, confused with the fraction lost. The process in which 1 photon creates 2 or more pairs occurs only slightly in silicon with ultraviolet light and hardly at all with 500 nm light, so the loss is not almost 0%. Reducing this thermalization loss is the idea behind tandem solar cells, which stack cells with different bandgaps.

photovoltaics-010.question: Which is a property of a solar cell whose open-circuit voltage is close to the theoretical limit?
choices: The less light it emits in the open-circuit state the better, since materials that emit light on recombination lose more of the generated power and so have a lower open-circuit voltage
In the open-circuit state all carriers recombine inside the cell, so the open-circuit voltage is higher the less non-radiative recombination and the higher the external luminescence efficiency
The open-circuit voltage is set by the bandgap alone (about 1.12 V for silicon) and does not depend on the kind of recombination, the luminescence efficiency or non-radiative losses
photovoltaics-010.explanation: In the open-circuit state no current is extracted, so all generated carriers recombine inside the cell. If recombination is purely radiative, the carrier density stays as high as possible and the open-circuit voltage reaches the detailed-balance limit. Non-radiative recombination removes carriers sooner and lowers the open-circuit voltage by (kT/q)|ln ηext|, where ηext is the external luminescence efficiency; at ηext = 1% it is about 0.12 V lower at 300 K. Photon recycling, in which photons from radiative recombination are reabsorbed, also helps, so high-efficiency GaAs cells are designed for light extraction as well. Emitting light is not itself a loss; recombination that turns into heat without emitting light is what lowers the open-circuit voltage. The open-circuit voltage is always below the bandgap divided by q, and the difference is set by recombination.

photovoltaics-011.question: Which correctly describes how the external quantum efficiency (EQE, the number of electrons delivered to the external circuit per incident photon) of a crystalline silicon solar cell varies with wavelength?
choices: At long wavelengths absorption is weak and incomplete, so it falls toward about 1100 nm, and at short wavelengths it falls through losses to surface recombination
EQE is proportional to photon energy, so it rises toward shorter wavelengths and peaks for ultraviolet light absorbed near the surface
EQE is constant at all wavelengths shorter than the bandgap wavelength, does not include the effects of surface reflection or incomplete absorption, and does not depend on cell thickness
photovoltaics-011.explanation: EQE is the ratio of electrons to photons that includes all losses from reflection, incomplete absorption and carrier collection. Silicon is an indirect semiconductor whose absorption coefficient is small at wavelengths near the bandgap, about 1100 nm, so a cell 100-odd µm thick cannot absorb all the light, and light trapping that lengthens the light path with surface texture and rear reflection is effective. Ultraviolet and blue light is absorbed within roughly 0.5 µm of the surface, so it is more exposed to losses from surface recombination and heavily doped layers. The value expressed per absorbed photon, excluding reflection, is the internal quantum efficiency (IQE). Because it is a ratio of photon counts, it does not rise in proportion to photon energy, and it is a different quantity from responsivity per unit power.

photovoltaics-012.question: Of AM1.5G sunlight (1000 W/m²), take the number of photons with energy above the bandgap of silicon (1.12 eV) to be 2.7×10¹⁷ /(cm²·s). Which is closest to the short-circuit current density of a cell whose average external quantum efficiency for these photons is 90%? (q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C.)
choices: About 43 mA/cm²
About 3.9 mA/cm²
About 39 mA/cm²
photovoltaics-012.explanation: The short-circuit current density is the number of electrons extracted times the elementary charge: J_sc = qΦ × EQE = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 2.7×10¹⁷ × 0.90 ≈ 3.9×10⁻² A/cm², about 39 mA/cm². About 43 mA/cm² takes the external quantum efficiency as 100%, which corresponds to the upper limit of an ideal cell with no reflection or recombination. About 3.9 mA/cm² is off by one order of magnitude in converting A to mA. In reality the external quantum efficiency varies with wavelength, so J_sc = q∫EQE(λ)Φ(λ)dλ is obtained by multiplying the measured EQE spectrum by the photon numbers of the standard spectrum and summing, which is also used to check the current measured with a solar simulator.

photovoltaics-013.question: Which correctly describes a tandem solar cell in which 2 cells with different bandgaps are stacked from the illuminated side and connected in series with 2 terminals?
choices: The larger-bandgap cell is placed on the illuminated side; the voltage is roughly the sum of both, but the current is limited by the weaker cell, so the currents are matched
The cell with the smaller bandgap is placed on the illuminated side to absorb a wide range of wavelengths first, and the light it transmits is used by the lower cell with the larger bandgap
The currents of the 2 cells add while the voltage equals that of the lower-voltage cell, so the bandgaps are chosen close to each other to match the open-circuit voltages of the 2 cells
photovoltaics-013.explanation: Placing the larger-bandgap cell on top lets high-energy photons be used at a high voltage, reducing thermalization loss. Light transmitted by the top cell is absorbed by the lower, smaller-bandgap cell. If the smaller-bandgap cell were on top, it would absorb almost all the light and none would reach the lower cell. In a 2-terminal series connection the same current flows through both cells, so the voltages add, but the current is set by the weaker cell; for example, if the top cell gives 19 mA/cm² and the bottom 21 mA/cm², only about 19 mA/cm² can be extracted. The thickness or bandgap of the top cell is therefore adjusted to equalize the currents (current matching). A 4-terminal configuration with separate terminals for each cell does not need current matching.

photovoltaics-014.question: Which is correct about solar cells that use metal halide perovskites (for example CH₃NH₃PbI₃ or compositional variants) as the absorber layer?
choices: They are indirect semiconductors with small absorption coefficients, so, like silicon, they need layers 100 µm or more thick to absorb light and cannot be made by coating
Even slight crystal defects stop them from generating power, so, like silicon, they can only be made by growing single crystals at high temperature
The bandgap can be tuned through the halogen composition, suiting them to the top cell of a tandem with silicon, but stability against moisture, heat and light is a challenge
photovoltaics-014.explanation: Halide perovskites are direct-gap materials with large absorption coefficients, so films a few hundred nm thick absorb sunlight well, and the films can be made by solution coating or low-temperature evaporation. Even in polycrystalline films, most defects form shallow levels near the band edges and do little harm (defect tolerance), which together with the long carrier diffusion lengths is considered a reason for their high efficiency. Replacing iodine with bromine widens the bandgap, so in a tandem with silicon (1.12 eV) they can form a top cell of around 1.7 eV. On the other hand, decomposition and ion migration caused by moisture, heat and light lead to degradation, and ion migration also causes hysteresis, in which the I-V curve changes with scan direction and speed, so the output is checked by tracking the maximum power point for some time.

photovoltaics-015.question: A solar cell with an ideality factor of 1 receives light concentrated 100 times by a lens (100 suns). If the short-circuit current is proportional to light intensity and the cell is held at 300 K (kT/q = 0.0259 V), which is closest to the change in open-circuit voltage?
choices: It rises by about 0.05 V
It rises by about 0.12 V
It does not change (only the current becomes 100 times larger)
photovoltaics-015.explanation: Since V_oc ≈ (kT/q) ln(J_sc/J₀), a 100-fold J_sc raises V_oc by (kT/q) ln100 = 0.0259 × 4.61 ≈ 0.12 V. The power grows by the factor of 100 in current plus the rise in voltage, so if series-resistance losses are small, the conversion efficiency rises too. About 0.05 V wrongly uses the common logarithm log₁₀100 = 2. The open-circuit voltage grows with the logarithm of the current, so saying it does not change is also wrong. In practical concentrator systems, series-resistance loss from the large current and cell heating must be kept down, and lenses can collect only direct sunlight arriving from one direction, so a mount that tracks the sun is also needed. High-concentration systems use high-efficiency III-V multijunction cells.
